ARTEFACT: Movable archaeological finds or object-like remains. Include pottery, tools, jewellery, coins, inscriptions, figurines, vessels, detached architectural members, fragments, bones, ash, burnt bones, and other excavated remains when they are reported as finds or contents of a context. Annotate the full object phrase when a descriptive word forms the find type, but keep material and period words separate as MATERIAL or PERIOD when they only describe what the object is made of or when it dates from. Do not annotate immovable structures as ARTEFACT.
PERIOD: Archaeological periods, chronological phases, cultural phases, and ancient date ranges. Include the whole chronological expression, including prepositions such as «από», «ως», when they are part of the dating span. Annotate ancient centuries, date ranges, and named phases; exclude modern excavation years and modern historical dates.
LOCATION: Named geographical places and toponyms, not structures or persons. Include cities, villages, regions, countries, islands, bays, rivers, museums, ancient place names, and named geographic expressions. If the phrase denotes a place where a site is located, use LOCATION. If the phrase denotes an archaeological building, sanctuary, tomb, wall, room, well, altar, or other in situ structure, use CONTEXT instead.
CONTEXT: Immovable archaeological contexts, findspots, and in situ structures: temples, sanctuaries, wells, walls, tombs, rooms, altars, stoas, acropoleis, cemeteries, deposits, foundations, and named monuments. Annotate the full specific context phrase, including attached dedicatory or naming complements when they define the monument. Do not annotate broad generic words or modern fieldwork terms unless they refer to a specific archaeological context containing or associated with finds. Do not use CONTEXT for named places.
MATERIAL: Substances, raw materials, and material adjectives from which artefacts or structures are made, such as stone, clay, bronze, bone, shell, and material adjectives. Annotate only the material word or material phrase, not broad generic phrases such as «πρώτες ύλες». If ash, bones, ceramics, or similar remains are described as excavated finds or contents of a deposit, annotate them as ARTEFACT rather than MATERIAL.
SPECIES: Animal and plant names, including mythological animals, when they denote living creatures or represented creatures. If an animal or plant term denotes the material of an object, annotate it as MATERIAL instead.
PERSON: Named historical, mythological, or divine figures when they are mentioned as persons or represented figures. Exclude modern archaeologists, researchers, authors, and excavators. When a deity's name is part of the official name of a sanctuary, temple, or other monument, include it inside the CONTEXT phrase rather than tagging the deity separately as PERSON or LOCATION.
FEATURE: Stylistic, typological, iconographic, technical, shape, decoration, or form characteristics of artefacts or contexts. Annotate feature words when they describe form, type, decoration, or iconography. Do not tag general narrative concepts, materials, periods, persons, or whole artefact names as FEATURE. If a word is part of a conventional artefact type, prefer ARTEFACT for the object phrase.
